title: Two-register groups: integer, reduction, cast, memory and complex
surface: Reg(dtype, reg_num=2) and MaskReg(dtype, reg_num=2); MaskReg.update(count) tails; vand / vmod / muldstadd / shiftrs; Reg.arange; interleave / deinterleave and mask_interleave; ub_to_reg_gather / reg_to_ub_scatter; cast with CastConfig(round_mode=RoundMode.TRUNC); complex32 and complex64 registers
study_for: A group is one logical register over two physical ones, and the masks cross that seam on purpose. `reg_num=2` gives 512 bytes; the int64 tails are 47 lanes and the complex32 one is 95, so each crosses the single-register boundary (32 and 64 respectively). An implementation that applied a mask only to the first physical register passes a 32-lane test and fails every case here.

The memory variant puts two different mask semantics side by side. A masked gather clears the lanes it did not fill; a masked scatter leaves untouched destination lanes exactly as they were, which is why the kernel calls `d.fill(0)` and publishes that zero before scattering into it. Reading those three rows together is the cheapest way to learn which of the two you are dealing with.

`deinterleave(d, e, d, e)` aliases its outputs onto its inputs, and both original halves still have to be read before either is written. The row pair before it holds the interleaved values, so the recovery is checked against the original inputs rather than against a claim that the operation is reversible.

The integer ramps are based at +/-18014398509481991, past 2^54. That is a statement about the reference as much as about the kernel: a reference that computed the ramp in float64 would round the low bits away and then agree with an implementation that had also lost them. The reference builds the ramp from Python integers.

Everything is compared as `uint8` carriers. The destinations include `complex32`, `complex64` and `uint64`; concatenating their bytes is what lets one comparison cover both components of every complex lane, the low bits of every wide integer, and each lane a mask left inactive -- with a poison of 97 in every destination, so an unwritten byte is distinguishable from a deliberately cleared one.
do_not_copy_when: You are counting on a masked scatter to zero what it skipped. It does not. The destination is yours to initialise, and this unit only gets a defined answer because it does.

You are treating the non-leading reduction lanes as a device guarantee. Rows 0 to 2 of the reduce variant hold their result in lane 0 and zero elsewhere in the model; a model check does not by itself establish that on silicon.

You need the complex variants on a backend other than CCE. Their kernels say so: hardware backend support is CCE only. The PTO complex-type refusal and the PyPTO grouped-register refusal are located by the backend tests, not here, and a green run of this unit says nothing about either.

You want a single-register example. Every register here is a group, and several of the assertions exist only because it is. For the single-register behaviour of the same operations, the mask extents and boundaries would all be different numbers.
